subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students
title: The Bode Plot That Lost 20 dB in One Decade
featured_title: THE BODE PLOT THAT LOST 20 DB IN ONE DECADE

presentation.challenge: The low-frequency gain was 40 dB. One decade past the pole, the response was near 20 dB.

practice.primary_question: Why does a first-order pole make the Bode magnitude slope decrease by 20 dB per decade?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Treating low-frequency gain as flat at all frequencies and ignoring the pole's -20 dB/decade contribution.

case_dna.target_misconception: If a transfer function has DC gain 100, its magnitude remains 40 dB well above its pole.
case_dna.why_plausible: The 20log10(K) calculation is correct at low frequency, but it is easy to forget the frequency-dependent denominator.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: For H(s)=100/(1+s/10), the pole is 10 rad/s. At 100 rad/s, |H|=100/sqrt(1+10^2)≈9.95, or about 20 dB.
case_dna.corrected_model: A first-order pole contributes approximately -20 dB/decade above its corner frequency and -45° phase at the corner.

problem_statement: A first-order system has H(s)=100/(1+s/10). A technician plots a flat 40 dB magnitude because the numerator gain is 100. Measurement is about 37 dB at 10 rad/s and 20 dB at 100 rad/s. Diagnose the missing pole behavior, calculate the magnitude at 100 rad/s, and identify the asymptotic slope above the corner.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The 40 dB line collapsed after 10 rad/s.
facts: Measured magnitude at 10 rad/s: about 37 dB
Measured magnitude at 100 rad/s: about 20 dB
gates.prompt: What does the first-order pole contribute above its corner frequency?

options.label: The pole adds a -20 dB/decade slope above 10 rad/s
options.reason: Each first-order pole contributes approximately -20 dB/decade after its corner.

options.label: The response stays flat at 40 dB because K=100
options.reason: That ignores the denominator's frequency dependence.

options.label: The pole adds +20 dB/decade
options.reason: A pole reduces magnitude; a zero increases it.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict magnitude one decade above the pole
gates.prompt: Using the asymptotic Bode rule, what magnitude (dB) do you expect near 100 rad/s?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Sweep to 100 rad/s
gates.result: The magnitude is approximately 20 dB at 100 rad/s.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Calculate the exact magnitude
gates.prompt: At ω=100 rad/s, use |H|=100/sqrt(1+(ω/10)^2), then convert to dB. Enter the dB magnitude.

cards.text: At the corner, magnitude is 3 dB below the low-frequency asymptote.
One decade above the pole, the asymptote has fallen about 20 dB.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the Bode sketch
report: C1. The low-frequency gain is 40 dB.
C2. The system has a pole at 10 rad/s.
C3. Therefore the magnitude remains 40 dB above 10 rad/s.

claims.label: C1
claims.reason: 100 corresponds to 40 dB at low frequency.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: The denominator gives a pole at 10 rad/s.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: A first-order pole introduces -20 dB/decade above the corner.

evidence_choices.label: At 100 rad/s, |H|≈9.95, which is about 20 dB

correction.template: Above the 10 rad/s pole, the magnitude asymptote has a {slope} dB/decade slope.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Move the roll-off to a higher frequency
gates.constraint: Keep the same DC gain of 100.

options.label: Move the pole from 10 rad/s to 100 rad/s
options.reason: That extends the approximately flat low-frequency region by one decade.

options.label: Reduce K from 100 to 10
options.reason: That reduces DC gain but does not move the corner frequency.

options.label: Add another pole at 10 rad/s
options.reason: That makes the high-frequency roll-off steeper.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the pole-slope rule
gates.prompt: A transfer function has two first-order poles and no zeros. What is the high-frequency asymptotic slope after both poles?

options.label: -20 dB/decade
options.reason: That accounts for only one pole.

gates.explanation: Bode magnitude slopes add algebraically: two poles contribute -40 dB/decade.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the Bode correction
gates.confirmation: I confirm that each first-order pole reduces the high-frequency Bode magnitude slope by 20 dB per decade.

items.label: What failed
items.value: A 40 dB DC gain was incorrectly extended to all frequencies.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: The pole at 10 rad/s changes the frequency response.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use the corner frequency and pole/zero slope contributions when sketching Bode magnitude.

seo.seo_title: Bode Plot First-Order Pole: Why 40 dB Falls to 20 dB | FE E-033
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-033: a first-order pole at 10 rad/s turns a 40 dB low-frequency gain into about 20 dB at 100 rad/s.
seo.focus_keyphrase: Bode plot first order pole FE exam
seo.excerpt: A DC gain of 100 gives 40 dB only in the low-frequency region. A first-order pole changes the slope above its corner.
seo.direct_answer: A first-order pole contributes approximately -20 dB per decade above its corner frequency. For H(s)=100/(1+s/10), the magnitude is 40 dB at low frequency, about 37 dB at 10 rad/s, and about 20 dB at 100 rad/s.

faqs.q: What Bode magnitude slope does one pole add?
faqs.a: Approximately -20 dB per decade above the pole frequency.

faqs.q: How far below the asymptote is a first-order pole at its corner?
